name: 4Ps of Marketing
one_line_summary: McCarthy's product, price, place, promotion as the four levers of marketing.
extended_summary: The 4Ps of Marketing was articulated by E. Jerome McCarthy in his 1960 textbook Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach, providing a memorable mnemonic for the marketing-mix concept that Neil Borden had previously articulated in 1953-1964 as a longer list of 12 elements. McCarthy's compression to four manageable categories — Product (the offering: features, design, branding, packaging, support); Price (the exchange terms: list price, discounts, financing, payment terms); Place (distribution: channels, locations, logistics, inventory); Promotion (communication: advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, direct marketing) — became the dominant framework for marketing decisions and persists as the foundational vocabulary of marketing education globally despite many subsequent extensions and alternatives. The framework's central commitment is that marketing decisions can be analyzed and coordinated as a 'mix' of controllable elements, with the marketing manager's task being to select the right combination for the target market. The 4Ps shaped marketing-discipline development through the 1960s-1990s as marketing established itself as a managerial discipline distinct from sales, economics, and consumer behavior. Subsequent extensions (7Ps for services, 4Cs from customer perspective) and alternatives (Ehrenberg-Bass empirical-laws approach) respond to the framework's perceived limitations while typically retaining the 4Ps vocabulary.
originators: E. Jerome McCarthy (4Ps formulation); Neil Borden (marketing-mix concept antecedent)
core_components: Four controllable marketing elements: Product, Price, Place, Promotion; Marketing-mix concept (selecting the right combination for target market); Distinction from earlier sales-oriented framings; Connection to STP (Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning) as upstream decisions; Foundation for marketing decisions and budget allocation; Subsequent extensions (7Ps, 4Cs); Substantial pedagogical role in marketing education; Distinction from purely strategic frameworks (4Ps focus on tactical execution)
primary_use_case: Foundational marketing framework taught in essentially every marketing curriculum globally; basis for marketing decision-making and resource allocation; reference framework for marketing-mix planning; foundation for many marketing-strategy textbooks and certifications; pedagogical mnemonic for introducing marketing to non-specialists; basis for marketing audits and analyses across industries.
common_criticisms: Producer-centric framing (decisions made by the marketer, not understood from customer view) led to development of 4Cs alternative (Lauterborn 1990); 4Ps inadequate for services-marketing (where intangibility, perishability, inseparability, variability create distinctive challenges) led to 7Ps extension (Booms-Bitner 1981); the framework is descriptive of marketing-decision categories but not prescriptive — it doesn't tell you what to do with each P; tactical orientation can underweight strategic positioning that determines which 4Ps choices make sense; difficulty in coordinating across the four Ps in real organizations where different functions own each; Ehrenberg-Bass empirical research has challenged some 4Ps-implicit assumptions about customer responsiveness to marketing-mix variation; commercial popularization has produced 4Ps as decoration on marketing plans without substantive analytical engagement; tension between 4Ps as analytical framework and 4Ps as branding language for marketing curricula.
primary_sources: Borden, N.H. (1964). 'The Concept of the Marketing Mix', Journal of Advertising Research; McCarthy, E.J. (1960, multiple editions). Basic Marketing: A Managerial Approach; Kotler, P. (multiple editions). Marketing Management

name: 7Ps of Marketing
one_line_summary: Booms and Bitner's extension adding people, process, and physical evidence for services.
extended_summary: The 7Ps of Marketing was articulated by Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner in their 1981 paper 'Marketing Strategies and Organization Structures for Service Firms' as an extension of McCarthy's 4Ps to address the distinctive characteristics of services that the original framework underweighted. The four characteristics of services that motivate the extension are intangibility (services cannot be touched or stored), perishability (services consumed at the moment of production cannot be inventoried), inseparability (production and consumption typically simultaneous), and variability (services vary substantially across providers and even occasions). The three additional Ps address these characteristics: People — the human actors performing and receiving the service (employees, customers, other customers in the experience); Process — the procedures, mechanisms, and flow of activities by which the service is delivered; Physical Evidence — the tangible cues (environment, brochures, equipment, decor) that signal service quality before and during consumption. The 7Ps framework dominates services-marketing education and has been substantially adopted in industries including hospitality, healthcare, education, financial services, and professional services. The framework retains the 4Ps strengths and weaknesses while addressing services-specific concerns; it has been substantially complemented by Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo-Lusch 2004) and other contemporary services-marketing developments.
originators: Bernard H. Booms; Mary Jo Bitner
core_components: Original 4Ps: Product, Price, Place, Promotion; Three additional Ps for services: People (employees, customers); Process (procedures and flow); Physical Evidence (tangible cues); Connection to four characteristics of services: intangibility, perishability, inseparability, variability; Distinction from goods-marketing emphasis; Foundation of services-marketing as distinct discipline; Subsequent complement by Service-Dominant Logic and service-design frameworks
primary_use_case: Services-marketing analysis and planning; foundation for hospitality, healthcare, education, financial services, professional services marketing; reference framework in services-marketing education and certification; basis for service-blueprinting and service-design practice; integration with customer-experience management.
common_criticisms: Inherits 4Ps producer-centric framing concerns; substantial conceptual overlap among the three additional Ps (People-Process-Physical Evidence often interact in ways the framework doesn't fully resolve); some services-marketing scholars argue the goods-services distinction is less fundamental than the 7Ps assumes — Service-Dominant Logic (Vargo-Lusch) reframes all marketing as service-marketing; framework less adopted in pure-product contexts; commercial certification industry has produced compliance-style 7Ps adoption; 'Physical Evidence' is awkward category that overlaps with environmental psychology in ways the framework doesn't fully integrate; like the 4Ps, descriptive rather than prescriptive — doesn't tell you what to do with each P; modern digital and platform services raise questions about how to operationalize Place and Physical Evidence.
primary_sources: Booms, B.H. & Bitner, M.J. (1981). 'Marketing Strategies and Organization Structures for Service Firms', in Donnelly & George (eds.) Marketing of Services; Lovelock, C. & Wirtz, J. (multiple editions). Services Marketing

name: 4Cs of Marketing
one_line_summary: Lauterborn's customer-centric reframe: consumer, cost, convenience, communication.
extended_summary: The 4Cs of Marketing was articulated by Robert F. Lauterborn in his 1990 Advertising Age article 'New Marketing Litany: Four Ps Passé; C-Words Take Over' as a customer-centric reframing of McCarthy's producer-centric 4Ps. Each C corresponds to a P viewed from the customer's perspective: Customer (or Consumer wants and needs) replaces Product — what does the customer actually want, not what does the producer want to sell; Cost (to the customer) replaces Price — total cost including time, effort, and switching costs, not just monetary price; Convenience replaces Place — how easily can the customer access the offering, not where does the producer want to distribute; Communication replaces Promotion — two-way dialogue rather than one-way producer-to-customer broadcasts. The framework reflects broader 1980s-1990s marketing developments emphasizing customer orientation, relationship marketing (Berry, Levitt), and dialogue-based marketing communication. The 4Cs gained substantial adoption particularly in marketing-strategy contexts emphasizing customer experience and digital marketing where two-way communication became central. The framework is typically presented as complement rather than replacement to the 4Ps — the same marketing-mix decisions analyzed from two perspectives. More recent extensions including the 7Cs (adding Credibility, Connection, Conversation in some formulations) have elaborated the customer-centric framing further.
core_components: Four customer-centric elements: Customer (replaces Product), Cost (replaces Price), Convenience (replaces Place), Communication (replaces Promotion); Reframing of 4Ps from customer perspective; Connection to customer orientation and relationship marketing; Two-way Communication as alternative to one-way Promotion; Total Cost concept (beyond monetary price); Subsequent extensions (7Cs and others); Typically complement rather than replacement to 4Ps
primary_use_case: Customer-centric marketing analysis particularly in service and digital contexts; complement to 4Ps in marketing strategy; foundation for customer-experience design and journey mapping; reference framework in customer-relationship-management literature; basis for some marketing-audit frameworks; integration with contemporary digital marketing where two-way communication is central.
common_criticisms: Translation of 4Ps to 4Cs is sometimes mechanical without substantive customer insight — relabeling Promotion as Communication doesn't automatically produce two-way dialogue; the reframing addresses 4Ps' producer-centric language but doesn't fundamentally change the categorical structure; multiple competing customer-centric reframings (4Cs has at least three distinct versions including Lauterborn's, Schultz et al.'s integrated marketing communications framing, and the Communication framework variant); commercial adoption sometimes treats 4Cs as alternative to 4Ps rather than complement, producing confusion; like 4Ps, descriptive rather than prescriptive about which customer needs to address; framework's effectiveness depends substantially on actual customer research that goes beyond renaming categories; 'Cost' as total cost is conceptually rich but operationally challenging.
primary_sources: Lauterborn, R.F. (1990). 'New Marketing Litany: Four Ps Passé; C-Words Take Over', Advertising Age; Schultz, D.E., Tannenbaum, S.I. & Lauterborn, R.F. (1993). Integrated Marketing Communications

name: AIDA
one_line_summary: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — classic linear advertising response model.
extended_summary: AIDA is the foundational hierarchy-of-effects model in advertising and selling, articulating the sequence of mental states a prospect must traverse to become a customer: Attention (awareness of the product or message), Interest (engagement with what the product offers), Desire (wanting the product), Action (purchase or commitment). The framework is conventionally attributed to St. Elmo Lewis, who articulated something close to it in 1898-1899 in his work as a successful Philadelphia advertising practitioner; the specific 'AIDA' acronym emerged later through the work of E. K. Strong (The Psychology of Selling, 1925) and others. AIDA became foundational to 20th-century advertising practice and selling methodology, providing a structure for evaluating advertisements (does this ad get attention? does it create interest?...) and for organizing sales conversations. The framework's central commitment is that persuasion is a sequential cognitive process, with each stage gating the next, and that marketing communications should be designed to advance prospects through the sequence. AIDA has been substantially extended (AIDAS adding Satisfaction, AIDCA adding Conviction, AIDA(R) adding Retention/Loyalty), reframed as the Marketing Funnel, and challenged by contemporary marketing science (notably Ehrenberg-Bass empirical work) that disputes the sequential-cognitive-process foundation. The framework's pedagogical durability vastly exceeds its empirical validation.
originators: St. Elmo Lewis (foundational articulation, 1898-1899); E. K. Strong (specific acronym formulation, 1925)
core_components: Four sequential stages: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action; Hierarchy-of-effects assumption (each stage gates the next); Application to advertisements and sales conversations; Foundation for many subsequent funnel and journey models; Subsequent extensions (AIDAS, AIDCA, AIDA(R)); Connection to Marketing Funnel; Distinction from contemporary empirical-marketing approaches that challenge sequential-cognitive assumptions; Substantial pedagogical role despite empirical concerns
primary_use_case: Foundational framework in advertising and sales education; basis for evaluating advertisements and organizing sales conversations; pedagogical mnemonic for introducing persuasion sequence; reference framework in copywriting and direct-response marketing; foundation for Marketing Funnel and many subsequent stage-based marketing models; influence well beyond marketing into broader communication training.
common_criticisms: Hierarchy-of-effects assumption that persuasion proceeds sequentially through cognitive states has been substantially challenged by empirical research (Ehrenberg-Bass work, Vakratsas-Ambler 1999 'How Advertising Works' review) — much consumer behavior is habit-based, low-involvement, or driven by mental availability rather than sequential cognitive engagement; the framework predicts that marketing must move prospects through stages, but empirical work suggests effective marketing often works by maintaining mental and physical availability rather than through deep cognitive engagement; the AIDA stages are not empirically operationalized in standard ways across studies; popular use often deploys AIDA as decorative structure rather than analytical framework; cross-cultural variation in persuasion processes underweighted; the framework's age (125+ years) may exceed its contemporary applicability; commercial copywriting industry has produced AIDA as conventional structure that may not reflect actual consumer behavior.
primary_sources: Lewis, E. St. Elmo (various articles 1898-1899 in The Inland Printer); Strong, E.K. (1925). The Psychology of Selling and Advertising; Vakratsas, D. & Ambler, T. (1999). 'How Advertising Works: What Do We Really Know?', Journal of Marketing (critical review)

name: AIDAS
one_line_summary: AIDA extended with Satisfaction to capture post-purchase loyalty.
extended_summary: AIDAS extends the classic AIDA framework by adding a fifth stage — Satisfaction — addressing the post-purchase phase that the original AIDA implicitly ended at Action (purchase). The Satisfaction stage recognizes that customer-relationship value extends beyond the initial transaction: a satisfied customer becomes a repeat purchaser, recommends the product to others (word-of-mouth, referral), and is less susceptible to competitor switching. The extension is conventionally attributed to selling-process literature in the mid-20th century, with the specific AIDAS acronym appearing in various selling textbooks from the 1960s onward, though the underlying recognition that selling continues after the sale was substantially developed by Theodore Levitt (Marketing Myopia, 1960) and the broader relationship-marketing tradition. AIDAS reflects the broader 20th-century shift from transactional to relationship-based marketing thinking. The framework retains AIDA's hierarchy-of-effects assumptions and inherits its critiques, but addresses the substantial real-world fact that marketing investments are best evaluated against customer lifetime value rather than initial-transaction conversion. Contemporary developments including Net Promoter Score, Customer Lifetime Value frameworks, and customer-success movements substantially extend AIDAS's post-purchase concerns into structured discipline.
originators: Selling-process literature (mid-20th century, no single inventor); broader relationship-marketing tradition including Theodore Levitt; subsequent customer-success movement
year_or_decade: 1960s onward (specific acronym in selling textbooks); foundational concepts older
core_components: Original AIDA stages: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action; Fifth stage: Satisfaction (post-purchase customer experience and loyalty); Connection to relationship marketing tradition; Recognition that selling continues after sale; Foundation for repeat-purchase and word-of-mouth thinking; Connection to Customer Lifetime Value frameworks; Connection to Net Promoter Score and customer-success movements
primary_use_case: Sales-training and selling-process frameworks particularly in B2B contexts; basis for relationship-marketing thinking; foundation for some customer-success methodologies; reference framework in selling and customer-relationship-management literature; complement to AIDA in marketing education that addresses post-purchase phase; integration with customer-experience management.
common_criticisms: Inherits AIDA's hierarchy-of-effects critiques — sequential-cognitive assumptions challenged by empirical research; specific 'AIDAS' acronym attribution is vague — no single inventor with clear claim, and selling-textbook literature varies in which extension acronym they prefer (AIDAS, AIDCAS, AIDCRA all appear); the framework treats Satisfaction as a stage rather than a continuing relationship dimension, which more sophisticated relationship-marketing frameworks address better; commercial selling-training industry has produced AIDAS as one of several similar mnemonic frameworks without clear empirical preference; 'Satisfaction' is operationally varied across implementations; the addition of one stage doesn't address AIDA's broader limitations about how marketing actually works; works principally in transactional-product contexts where 'satisfaction' has meaningful operational definition.
primary_sources: Various selling textbooks 1960s onward; broader relationship-marketing tradition including Levitt, T. (1960). 'Marketing Myopia', Harvard Business Review; Berry, L.L. (1983). 'Relationship Marketing'

name: STP
one_line_summary: Sequential approach: segment market, target chosen segments, position offering distinctively.
extended_summary: STP — Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning — is the foundational strategic-marketing framework that operates upstream of tactical 4Ps decisions, articulated principally by Philip Kotler in successive editions of Marketing Management (1967 onward) drawing on Wendell R. Smith's foundational 1956 article 'Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies'. The framework structures marketing strategy through three sequential decisions: (1) Segmentation — divide the heterogeneous market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs, behaviors, or characteristics, using bases including demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioral, and benefit-sought variables; (2) Targeting — evaluate the segments and select which to serve, considering segment size, growth, accessibility, and fit with company capabilities; (3) Positioning — develop a distinctive offering and communication that occupies a specific, valued position in target customers' minds relative to competitors. Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind (1981) substantially developed the third leg of STP into its own substantive theory. STP became the dominant strategic-marketing framework from the 1970s onward and remains foundational to marketing education and professional practice. The framework's central insight — that marketing strategy must precede tactical execution — distinguishes it from purely tactical 4Ps thinking. Recent challenges from Ehrenberg-Bass (Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow, 2010) include the empirical claim that mass-marketing brands grow primarily through penetration rather than through targeted segment-specific positioning, complicating STP's strategic prescriptions.
originators: Wendell R. Smith (segmentation foundational); Philip Kotler (STP integration); Al Ries and Jack Trout (positioning development)
year_or_decade: 1956 (Smith on segmentation); 1967 onward (Kotler integration in Marketing Management); 1981 (Ries-Trout Positioning)
core_components: Three sequential decisions: Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning; Segmentation bases: demographic, geographic, psychographic, behavioral, benefit-sought; Targeting evaluation: segment attractiveness, company fit; Positioning: distinctive valued position in target customers' minds; Connection to 4Ps as upstream strategic framework; Distinction from purely tactical 4Ps thinking; Influence of Ries-Trout positioning theory; Recent challenges from Ehrenberg-Bass empirical work on brand growth
primary_use_case: Foundational strategic-marketing framework; basis for marketing-plan development across industries; reference framework in marketing-strategy education; foundation for substantial marketing-research practice (segmentation studies); integration with brand-management practice; pedagogical sequence in marketing courses (STP before 4Ps).
common_criticisms: Ehrenberg-Bass research (Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow, 2010) has substantially challenged STP's strategic prescriptions — empirical evidence suggests brands grow primarily through penetration of broad markets rather than through targeted segment-specific positioning, and that 'targeted' brands often achieve their loyal customers as a consequence of size rather than as a strategic accomplishment; segmentation in practice is often based on convenient available data rather than on actual differential customer responsiveness, producing pseudosegmentation; positioning research has been argued to overstate the strategic importance of perceived differentiation; commercial segmentation-research industry has produced enormous output of varying analytical value; the sequential STP framing (segment first, then target, then position) doesn't always match strategic reality where positioning insights drive segmentation; works better for high-involvement product categories than for low-involvement everyday categories.
primary_sources: Smith, W.R. (1956). 'Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies', Journal of Marketing; Ries, A. & Trout, J. (1981). Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind; Kotler, P. (multiple editions). Marketing Management; Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow (challenge)

name: Marketing Funnel
one_line_summary: Awareness through purchase as a narrowing pipeline of prospects.
extended_summary: The Marketing Funnel is the family of stage-based models depicting customer progression from initial awareness of a product or category through evaluation and purchase to (in extended versions) advocacy and loyalty, conventionally depicted as a downward-narrowing funnel reflecting attrition at each stage. Variants are numerous: classic AIDA-derived (Awareness, Interest, Desire, Action); five-stage (Awareness, Consideration, Conversion, Retention, Advocacy); McKinsey's Consumer Decision Journey (2009, more circular than funnel-shaped); Pirate Metrics AARRR (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — separately enriched). The framework's pedagogical strength is the visual representation of attrition (most awareness doesn't convert to consideration; most consideration doesn't convert to purchase) and the implication that marketing must address each stage with appropriate content, channels, and metrics. The framework substantially shapes marketing-organization design (top-of-funnel teams responsible for awareness; bottom-of-funnel for conversion), measurement (funnel-conversion rates), and budget allocation. Substantial criticism includes that contemporary customer journeys are not linear (customers loop, abandon and return, evaluate non-sequentially), that the funnel framing privileges acquisition over retention, that empirical work (Ehrenberg-Bass, McKinsey) shows actual customer journeys differ from the funnel model, and that the framework's pedagogical durability exceeds its empirical validation. Despite these critiques, the funnel remains the dominant operational framework in B2B marketing and substantial parts of B2C.
originators: St. Elmo Lewis (AIDA foundation, 1898-1899); William W. Townsend (1924, often cited as funnel-specific articulation); subsequent ongoing development including McKinsey, Forrester, and digital-marketing community
year_or_decade: 1898-1899 (Lewis AIDA); 1924 (Townsend funnel-specific); ongoing development through 21st century
core_components: Sequential stages from awareness to (in some versions) advocacy; Funnel shape representing attrition at each stage; Multiple stage frameworks (AIDA-derived, five-stage, AARRR Pirate Metrics, McKinsey Consumer Decision Journey); Application to marketing-organization design and measurement; Funnel-conversion rate metrics; Top-of-funnel vs bottom-of-funnel content strategy; Distinction between B2B (longer, more rigid funnel) and B2C (shorter, often non-linear) applications; Substantial pedagogical durability despite empirical critiques
primary_use_case: Marketing-organization design and accountability (which team owns which stage); marketing-measurement frameworks (funnel-conversion analytics); content-strategy planning (top-of-funnel awareness content vs bottom-of-funnel conversion content); B2B sales-and-marketing alignment (lead-to-revenue funnel); foundation for marketing-automation platform design (HubSpot, Marketo, Pardot, Salesforce); pedagogical mnemonic in marketing education; basis for many digital-marketing analytics frameworks.
common_criticisms: Contemporary customer journeys are not linear — customers loop, abandon and return, evaluate non-sequentially, and engage with brands in ways that don't fit funnel-stage progression; McKinsey's 2009 'Consumer Decision Journey' research substantially documented this with empirical data showing actual decision processes differ from funnel; framework's acquisition focus underweights retention and customer-lifetime-value concerns; Ehrenberg-Bass empirical research challenges the sequential-cognitive-engagement assumptions underlying funnel thinking; commercial marketing-automation platform industry has shaped funnel adoption in ways that may not reflect actual customer behavior; B2B and B2C funnels differ substantially in ways often elided in popular treatments; 'top of funnel' vs 'bottom of funnel' has become organizational silo language rather than strategic distinction; metrics like 'funnel conversion rate' are sometimes optimized in ways that don't reflect underlying business value; framework's pedagogical durability vastly exceeds its empirical validation.
primary_sources: Lewis, E. St. Elmo (1898-1899). Various articles in The Inland Printer; Townsend, W.W. (1924). Bond Salesmanship; Court, D., Elzinga, D., Mulder, S. & Vetvik, O.J. (2009). 'The Consumer Decision Journey', McKinsey Quarterly (alternative)

name: Pirate Metrics
one_line_summary: McClure's Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue lifecycle for startups.
extended_summary: Pirate Metrics (AARRR) was articulated by Dave McClure (founder of 500 Startups) in a 2007 conference presentation at Web 2.0 Expo titled 'Startup Metrics for Pirates,' specifically targeted at consumer internet and SaaS startup contexts where traditional marketing-funnel thinking didn't fit the unit-economics and growth dynamics of digital products. The five stages: Acquisition (how do users find you? — channels, conversion rates, cost per acquisition); Activation (do users have a happy first experience? — onboarding, time-to-value, activation rate); Retention (do users come back? — engagement frequency, churn, cohort retention curves); Referral (do users tell others? — viral coefficient, referral rates, word-of-mouth); Revenue (do users monetize? — conversion to paid, average revenue per user, lifetime value). The framework's pirate-acronym memorability (AARRR — pronounced 'argh') contributed to its rapid adoption in startup and product-management communities. McClure's specific contribution was emphasizing Activation and Retention as critical stages that traditional marketing funnels underweighted — for many digital products, acquisition without activation produces no value, and retention without referral and monetization produces unsustainable economics. Pirate Metrics has been extensively adopted in startup, product-management, and growth-marketing communities and substantially influenced the rise of growth-hacking practice (Sean Ellis's coining of the term in 2010). The framework remains the dominant analytical framework for early-stage consumer-software product strategy.
core_components: Five stages: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue (AARRR); Specific application to consumer internet and SaaS contexts; Emphasis on Activation and Retention as critical stages; Connection to unit economics and lifetime-value thinking; Foundation for growth-hacking practice (Sean Ellis); Pirate-acronym memorability driving adoption; Distinction from traditional B2B marketing funnel; Cohort-based retention analysis; Connection to product-led growth movement
primary_use_case: Startup and consumer-software product analytics; foundation for growth-hacking and growth-marketing practice; basis for product-management metrics frameworks; reference framework in startup and product communities; foundation for many product-analytics platforms (Mixpanel, Amplitude); integration with cohort analysis and product-led growth thinking; basis for many startup-investor evaluation frameworks.
common_criticisms: Specific to consumer-internet and SaaS contexts — works less well for B2B, hardware, or high-touch enterprise sales where the funnel structure is fundamentally different; the framework's emphasis on Acquisition first can produce growth-at-all-costs strategies that exhaust unit economics; Sean Ellis later proposed RARRA (Retention, Activation, Referral, Revenue, Acquisition) reordering arguing Retention should come first; 'growth hacking' (descended substantially from Pirate Metrics thinking) has drawn substantial critique for ethical concerns about manipulation, dark patterns, and unsustainable acquisition tactics; commercial growth-marketing industry has produced compliance-style adoption of AARRR vocabulary without substantive analytical engagement; works principally for measurable digital products, less well for offline or relationship-driven businesses; tension between AARRR optimization and longer-term brand and customer-experience considerations.
primary_sources: McClure, D. (2007). 'Startup Metrics for Pirates' (Web 2.0 Expo presentation, subsequently widely shared); Ellis, S. (2010). 'Find a Growth Hacker for Your Startup' (related growth-hacking foundation); Croll, A. & Yoskovitz, B. (2013). Lean Analytics (substantial AARRR popularization)

name: Crossing the Chasm
one_line_summary: Moore's adaptation showing the gap between early adopters and early majority.
extended_summary: Crossing the Chasm was articulated by Geoffrey A. Moore in his 1991 book of the same name (revised editions through 2014), substantially extending Everett Rogers's Diffusion of Innovations adopter categories to high-tech product marketing. Moore's central insight was that Rogers's smooth S-curve obscures a critical discontinuity for technology products: a chasm exists between the Early Adopters (visionaries who buy on the basis of strategic potential, willing to tolerate immature products) and the Early Majority (pragmatists who buy on the basis of practical proven value, demanding mature products with established references). Many high-tech products gain initial traction with early adopters but fail to cross into mainstream market acceptance because the marketing approaches that work for early adopters (vision-selling, strategic partnership, technology-first) don't work for the early majority (who want references, complete products, and risk reduction). Moore's prescription: focus on a specific niche segment within the early majority where you can become the dominant solution (the 'beachhead' or 'D-Day strategy'), build whole-product completeness for that segment, accumulate references, and use those references to attack adjacent segments (the 'bowling alley'). The framework substantially shaped Silicon Valley product-marketing thinking from the 1990s onward and remains a foundational reference in B2B technology marketing, despite criticism that the chasm metaphor doesn't apply equally to all product categories and that successful technology companies often don't follow the bowling-alley prescription as Moore described.
core_components: The chasm: discontinuity between Early Adopters (visionaries) and Early Majority (pragmatists); Different buying psychology: visionaries vs pragmatists; Beachhead strategy: dominate one specific niche segment first; Whole-product completeness for the niche; Reference-driven adjacent-segment expansion (bowling alley, then tornado in subsequent Moore books); Connection to Rogers's Diffusion of Innovations; High-tech product context; Inside the Tornado (1995) and Living on the Fault Line (2000) as Moore's subsequent extensions
primary_use_case: B2B and high-tech product marketing; foundation for substantial Silicon Valley marketing thinking; basis for go-to-market strategy in technology startups and growth-stage companies; reference framework in technology product management; influence on venture-capital evaluation of startup go-to-market plans; integration with broader product-strategy frameworks; pedagogical reference in technology marketing education.
common_criticisms: Chasm metaphor doesn't apply equally to all product categories — consumer products often don't show the discontinuity Moore identified; successful technology companies often don't follow the bowling-alley prescription as Moore described, raising questions about whether the framework is descriptive or normative; Ehrenberg-Bass empirical research challenges the underlying targeting-based growth model that Crossing the Chasm shares with broader STP; specific historical examples Moore used have been argued to be retrofit rather than predictive; commercial application sometimes confuses 'crossing the chasm' with simply 'going from startup to growth stage' without engaging the specific buying-psychology distinction; the framework's age (1991) means it predates SaaS, freemium, product-led growth, and other contemporary go-to-market models that don't fit the original framing; Moore's subsequent books (Tornado, Fault Line) have varied reception suggesting the original Chasm framework was unusually robust; many B2B technology companies fail to cross the chasm despite explicit Chasm-based strategy, suggesting the framework identifies a real challenge but doesn't fully solve it.
primary_sources: Moore, G.A. (1991, 1999, 3rd ed. 2014). Crossing the Chasm: Marketing and Selling Disruptive Products to Mainstream Customers; Moore, G.A. (1995). Inside the Tornado

name: StoryBrand
one_line_summary: Donald Miller's seven-part brand-narrative framework casting customer as hero, brand as guide.
extended_summary: StoryBrand (or the SB7 Framework) was developed by Donald Miller and presented in Building a StoryBrand: Clarify Your Message So Customers Will Listen (2017). The framework applies narrative structure (substantially drawing on Joseph Campbell's hero's-journey monomyth as popularized by Christopher Vogler's The Writer's Journey) to marketing communications, structured around seven elements: (1) A Character (the customer, framed as the hero of the story); (2) Has a Problem (external problem, internal feelings, philosophical stakes); (3) Meets a Guide (the brand, positioned as helpful guide rather than as the hero); (4) Who Gives Them a Plan (process plan, agreement plan); (5) And Calls Them to Action (direct call, transitional call); (6) That Helps Them Avoid Failure (stakes if they don't act); (7) And Ends in Success (concrete vision of resolved life). Miller's central commitment is that marketing communications should make the customer the hero and the brand the guide — flipping the common pattern where the brand presents itself as the hero of its own story. StoryBrand has been substantially commercialized through Miller's StoryBrand consultancy, certified-guide network, and live-event business. The framework has gained widespread adoption in small-business and B2B marketing contexts, though it has drawn substantial critique for being more formulaic than its narrative-craft origins suggest and for producing template-driven marketing copy that may underweight category-specific marketing principles.
originators: Donald Miller (StoryBrand articulation); intellectual antecedents in Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey monomyth, Christopher Vogler's The Writer's Journey
core_components: Seven framework elements: Character, Problem, Guide, Plan, Call to Action, Failure (avoided), Success; Customer as hero, brand as guide; Three problem dimensions: external, internal, philosophical; Two plan types: process plan, agreement plan; Two CTA types: direct, transitional; Narrative-structure foundation in Campbell-Vogler hero's journey; Commercial certified-guide network; BrandScript document as canonical artifact; StoryBrand Marketing Workshop and consulting business
primary_use_case: Small-business marketing copywriting; B2B marketing message development; website and landing-page structure; sales-pitch development; reference framework in faith-based and values-driven business communities (Miller's audience originates partly in Christian-business contexts); foundation for many freelance copywriting and marketing-consulting practices; basis for the StoryBrand certified-guide network business model.
common_criticisms: Substantially template-driven application can produce homogeneous marketing copy across StoryBrand-trained agencies and consultancies; Ehrenberg-Bass empirical research challenges the assumption that distinctive narrative messaging drives brand growth (penetration through mental and physical availability matters more than message differentiation); the customer-as-hero framing oversimplifies — many real purchases don't fit hero's-journey structure (commodity purchases, habit-driven purchases, low-involvement decisions); commercial certified-guide industry has substantial financial incentive to produce StoryBrand applications regardless of fit with specific business contexts; the framework works principally for considered-purchase contexts where storytelling has room to operate, less well for everyday-product or commodity contexts; Miller's evangelical-Christian audience and framing has produced substantial overlap between StoryBrand and Christian-business movements that has not always traveled well to secular contexts; the formulaic 'fill in the BrandScript' application can substitute for genuine customer insight; underweights category-specific marketing principles (B2B differs from B2C, services from products, etc.).
primary_sources: Miller, D. (2017). Building a StoryBrand: Clarify Your Message So Customers Will Listen; Miller, D. (2021). Marketing Made Simple; Campbell, J. (1949). The Hero with a Thousand Faces (intellectual antecedent); Vogler, C. (1992). The Writer's Journey

name: Net Promoter Score
one_line_summary: Single-question loyalty measure based on likelihood to recommend.
extended_summary: Net Promoter Score (NPS) was articulated by Fred Reichheld of Bain & Company in his 2003 Harvard Business Review article 'The One Number You Need to Grow' (subsequently expanded in The Ultimate Question, 2006, and The Ultimate Question 2.0, 2011). NPS is calculated from responses to a single question: 'How likely are you to recommend [Company/Product] to a friend or colleague?' on a 0-10 scale. Respondents are categorized as Promoters (9-10), Passives (7-8), or Detractors (0-6); NPS = %Promoters minus %Detractors, producing a score between -100 and +100. Reichheld's original claim was that NPS correlates strongly with company growth and is a single sufficient metric for customer loyalty, replacing complex multi-question satisfaction surveys. NPS has been enormously commercially successful — adopted by thousands of companies as a standard customer-experience metric, with NPS scores reported quarterly to boards and tied to executive compensation in many organizations. However, NPS has drawn substantial published critique on multiple grounds: the original NPS-growth correlation has not replicated as strongly in independent studies (Keiningham et al. 2007, Sharp 2008, etc.); the 0-10 scale with the specific cutoffs is psychometrically peculiar; cross-cultural variation in scale usage produces misleading cross-country comparisons; and the metric's simplicity, while pedagogically attractive, oversimplifies customer-experience reality. Despite these critiques, NPS remains the most widely-used customer-loyalty metric.
core_components: Single question: 'How likely are you to recommend X to a friend or colleague?'; 0-10 scale; Categorization: Promoters (9-10), Passives (7-8), Detractors (0-6); Calculation: %Promoters minus %Detractors; Score range -100 to +100; Application as single customer-loyalty metric; Connection to follow-up question 'why did you give that score?'; tNPS (transactional NPS) and rNPS (relationship NPS) variants; Substantial commercial adoption (Bain consulting practice, Medallia, Qualtrics, others)
primary_use_case: Customer-experience measurement across industries; foundation for many customer-experience management programs; reference metric in many B2C and B2B contexts; basis for executive-compensation tie-ins to customer-experience performance; integration with customer-experience platforms (Medallia, Qualtrics, etc.); widespread board-level reporting metric; pedagogical simplicity drives adoption in customer-experience education.
common_criticisms: Substantial published critique: Keiningham, Cooil, Andreassen and Aksoy's 2007 'A Longitudinal Examination of Net Promoter and Firm Revenue Growth' found NPS-growth correlation weaker and less consistent than Reichheld's original claims; Byron Sharp and Ehrenberg-Bass research challenges NPS's underlying loyalty-as-key-driver assumptions; the specific 0-10 scale with the 9-10 Promoter cutoff is psychometrically peculiar — the categorization throws away information from neutral responses; cross-cultural variation in scale-usage habits produces misleading cross-country NPS comparisons (US respondents tend to use higher numbers than European or Asian respondents); NPS optimization can produce gaming behaviors (employees pleading for high scores); single-metric simplicity obscures important customer-experience dimensions that multi-metric approaches capture; despite the critiques, commercial adoption continues — the metric's pedagogical and reporting simplicity drives use even where validity is challenged; Reichheld himself has acknowledged some critiques and refined the framework in subsequent work, with NPS3 introducing 'earned growth rate' as supplementary metric.
primary_sources: Reichheld, F.F. (2003). 'The One Number You Need to Grow', Harvard Business Review; Reichheld, F.F. (2006). The Ultimate Question; Keiningham, T.L. et al. (2007). 'A Longitudinal Examination of Net Promoter and Firm Revenue Growth', Journal of Marketing (critique)

name: Customer Lifetime Value
one_line_summary: Projected revenue from a customer relationship over its entire duration.
extended_summary: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV or LTV) is the calculation of total expected revenue or profit a business will derive from a customer relationship over its expected duration, providing the principal financial framework for customer-acquisition cost decisions, retention investment, and customer-segment prioritization. The concept's origins are not from a single inventor — direct-marketing and database-marketing practitioners had been performing customer-economics calculations since at least the 1950s, with substantial codification through the 1980s-1990s database-marketing literature (Don Peppers, Martha Rogers, Frederick Reichheld, Sunil Gupta). The basic formula in its simplest form: CLV = (Average Order Value × Purchase Frequency × Customer Lifespan) - Customer Acquisition Cost, with substantial variants accounting for retention rate, discount rate (NPV-style time-value-of-money adjustment), gross margin rather than revenue, and probabilistic customer-state models (Schmittlein-Morrison-Colombo BG/NBD models, Pareto/NBD). The framework's central commitments include: customer relationships should be evaluated as portfolios of long-term cash flows; acquisition cost should be evaluated against expected lifetime value rather than first-purchase margin; not all customers are equally valuable, and segment-specific CLV calculations enable differentiated treatment. CLV has been particularly influential in subscription-business contexts (SaaS, telecom, banking, insurance) where contractual relationships make calculation more tractable. The framework has substantial implications when paired with Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), with the LTV/CAC ratio (typically aiming for 3:1 or higher in SaaS contexts) becoming a standard unit-economics metric.
originators: Direct-marketing practitioners since 1950s; substantial codification through database-marketing literature (Don Peppers, Martha Rogers, Frederick Reichheld, Sunil Gupta); academic development including David Schmittlein, Bruce Hardie, Peter Fader
year_or_decade: 1950s practitioner origins; 1990s academic and consulting development; ongoing refinement
core_components: Basic formula: (Average Order Value × Purchase Frequency × Customer Lifespan) - CAC; Variants accounting for retention rate, discount rate, gross margin; Probabilistic customer-state models (BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD — Schmittlein, Morrison, Colombo, Fader, Hardie); LTV/CAC ratio as unit-economics metric; Application particularly in subscription businesses; Connection to RFM Analysis and customer segmentation; Customer-acquisition-cost decisions; Foundation for many customer-success and retention investments
primary_use_case: Subscription-business unit economics (SaaS, telecom, financial services, media subscriptions); foundation for marketing-budget allocation across acquisition channels; basis for customer-segment prioritization; reference framework in venture-capital evaluation of growth-stage businesses; integration with customer-success and retention investment decisions; foundation for many customer-data-platform and analytics tools; pedagogical framework in marketing-finance education.
common_criticisms: Calculation is genuinely difficult — customer lifespan is uncertain, retention rates change over time, customer behavior varies in ways that aggregate calculations don't capture; commercial CLV implementations frequently rely on simplifying assumptions (constant retention rate, single-segment averages) that produce misleading estimates; Peter Fader and Bruce Hardie's substantial body of work has documented common CLV calculation errors and provided more rigorous probabilistic alternatives; LTV/CAC ratio targets (3:1, etc.) are often invoked as universal rules without engaging context-specific economics; in contractual subscription businesses CLV is more tractable than in non-contractual contexts where customer 'death' is unobservable; commercial CLV-software industry has produced compliance-style adoption with varying analytical fidelity; tendency to focus on highest-CLV segments can produce concentration risk and underweight broad-market growth opportunities (Ehrenberg-Bass concerns); cross-channel attribution complicates acquisition-cost calculations underlying CLV/CAC analysis; cohort-level CLV calculations are more reliable than per-customer estimates but often used interchangeably.
primary_sources: Peppers, D. & Rogers, M. (1993). The One to One Future; Reichheld, F.F. & Sasser, W.E. (1990). 'Zero Defections: Quality Comes to Services', HBR; Fader, P.S. & Hardie, B.G.S. (multiple papers). Probabilistic CLV models; Gupta, S. & Lehmann, D.R. (2005). Managing Customers as Investments

name: RFM Analysis
one_line_summary: Customer segmentation by how recently, how often, and how much they purchased.
extended_summary: RFM Analysis is the customer-segmentation technique that scores customers on three dimensions — Recency (how recently the customer last purchased), Frequency (how often the customer purchases), and Monetary (how much the customer spends) — and uses combined RFM scores to segment customers for differentiated marketing treatment. The technique originated in direct-marketing practice in the 1960s-1970s, with substantial codification through Jan R. Bult and Tom Wansbeek's academic work in the 1990s and earlier practitioner literature. Standard implementation: divide each dimension into typically 5 quintiles (1-5), producing a 555 'best customers' score down to 111 'inactive customers,' with 125 possible combinations enabling sophisticated segmentation. Practical applications include: identify high-value loyal customers for retention programs (high R, F, M); identify lapsed-but-previously-valuable customers for win-back campaigns (low R, high F and M historically); identify recently-acquired customers for nurturing (high R, low F); identify low-value customers for cost-management (low across dimensions). RFM works particularly well in transactional retail and direct-marketing contexts where the three dimensions are directly observable. The technique is conceptually simple, computationally tractable, and produces actionable segmentation, contributing to its enduring popularity despite the availability of more sophisticated probabilistic and machine-learning customer-segmentation approaches. RFM remains a foundational customer-segmentation reference taught in nearly every marketing-analytics course.
originators: Direct-marketing practitioner origins (1960s-1970s); substantial academic codification including Jan R. Bult, Tom Wansbeek, Arthur Hughes
year_or_decade: 1960s-1970s practitioner origins; 1990s academic codification; ongoing use
core_components: Three dimensions: Recency, Frequency, Monetary; Typically 5-point quintile scoring on each dimension; 555 to 111 combined scores producing 125 possible segments; Application to retention, win-back, nurture, cost-management; Particularly suited to transactional retail and direct-marketing contexts; Pedagogical and analytical simplicity; Connection to broader customer-segmentation methodologies; Foundation for many CRM and marketing-automation segmentation features
primary_use_case: Customer segmentation in retail, direct-marketing, e-commerce, and database-marketing contexts; foundation for many CRM-platform segmentation features; basis for differentiated email-marketing campaigns; reference framework in marketing-analytics education; integration with marketing-automation platforms; foundation for many customer-experience programs.
common_criticisms: Works principally in transactional contexts where Recency, Frequency, Monetary are directly observable — services, contractual subscriptions, and B2B contexts often require modified implementations; quintile-based scoring discards distributional information (a customer at the 25th percentile of monetary value is bucketed identically with one at the 19th percentile); cross-customer comparison assumes stable within-firm purchase patterns that may not hold across customer segments or product categories; more sophisticated probabilistic models (BG/NBD, Pareto/NBD) and machine-learning segmentation often outperform RFM on predictive accuracy, though at substantial complexity cost; RFM's simplicity, while pedagogically attractive, can lock organizations into segmentation approaches that don't reflect category-specific customer dynamics; commercial RFM implementations vary in quality and frequency of refresh; the technique is descriptive rather than predictive — high-RFM customers were valuable historically but may not remain so; cross-channel and omnichannel customer behavior creates RFM calculation challenges that single-channel implementations don't address.
