'Optimal Selection for Direct Mail', Marketing Science; Fader, P.S., Hardie, B.G.S. & Lee, K.L. (2005). 'RFM and CLV: Using Iso-Value Curves for Customer Base Analysis', Journal of Marketing Research
siblings: Customer Lifetime Value; Net Promoter Score

name: Means-End Theory
one_line_summary: Links product attributes to consumer values through a chain of consequences.
extended_summary: Means-End Theory was articulated by Jonathan Gutman in his 1982 Journal of Marketing paper 'A Means-End Chain Model Based on Consumer Categorization Processes,' building on Milton Rokeach's value-research tradition. The framework holds that consumers select products as 'means' to achieve desired 'ends' (personal values) through a chain of cognitive associations: product attributes (concrete physical features) lead to consequences (functional and psychosocial outcomes of using the product) which serve personal values (terminal values like security, accomplishment, belonging — the deepest motivational drivers). The chain is hierarchical: attributes → functional consequences → psychosocial consequences → instrumental values → terminal values. Marketing-research methodology developed to elicit means-end chains is principally the laddering interview (Reynolds and Gutman 1988), in which interviewers repeatedly ask 'why is that important to you?' to surface the cognitive chain from attribute to value. The framework's central commitment is that effective marketing communications should connect product attributes to the personal values customers actually care about, rather than focusing on attributes alone. Means-End Theory has been substantially influential in advertising-strategy development (the MECCAS model — Means-End Conceptualization of Components of Advertising Strategy), in qualitative marketing research, and in cross-cultural consumer research where value differences across cultures shape product evaluation. The framework remains a foundational reference in consumer-behavior education and qualitative marketing research, though it has drawn critique for relying on retrospective rationalization and for the substantial interpretive work required in laddering analysis.
originators: Jonathan Gutman (foundational); Thomas J. Reynolds (laddering methodology); intellectual antecedents in Milton Rokeach's value research
core_components: Hierarchical chain: attributes → functional consequences → psychosocial consequences → instrumental values → terminal values; Concrete to abstract progression; Connection to Rokeach's value research; Laddering interview methodology; MECCAS model for advertising strategy (Reynolds-Gutman 1984); Application to advertising development, brand positioning, qualitative consumer research; Distinction from purely attribute-focused or purely demographic marketing thinking; Cross-cultural variation in value chains
primary_use_case: Qualitative marketing research and consumer-insight development; advertising-strategy development through MECCAS model; brand-positioning research; cross-cultural consumer research; reference framework in consumer-behavior education; foundation for some psychographic-segmentation approaches; integration with values-based marketing.
common_criticisms: Laddering methodology relies on consumers' ability and willingness to articulate their motivations, which may produce retrospective rationalization rather than reflecting actual decision processes; substantial interpretive work required in laddering analysis introduces researcher subjectivity; the hierarchical chain structure assumes orderly cognition that may not match actual consumer decision-making (which is often habitual, low-involvement, or affective); cross-cultural application requires substantial cultural-knowledge investment that many implementations don't make; competing values-research traditions (Schwartz Value Survey, World Values Survey) offer different value taxonomies than Rokeach's; commercial qualitative-research industry has produced laddering applications of varying analytical fidelity; works better for high-involvement product categories (cars, financial services, healthcare) than for low-involvement everyday categories where deep value-chain analysis may be overkill; integration with quantitative methods has been incomplete; the framework's consumer-cognitive focus underweights social-influence and habit-driven dimensions of consumer behavior.
primary_sources: Gutman, J. (1982). 'A Means-End Chain Model Based on Consumer Categorization Processes', Journal of Marketing; Reynolds, T.J. & Gutman, J. (1984). 'Advertising Is Image Management', Journal of Advertising Research; Reynolds, T.J. & Gutman, J. (1988). 'Laddering Theory, Method, Analysis, and Interpretation', Journal of Advertising Research; Rokeach, M. (1973). The Nature of Human Values

name: Ehrenberg-Bass Laws
one_line_summary: Empirical regularities in buying behavior, including double jeopardy and brand penetration.
extended_summary: The Ehrenberg-Bass Laws are the body of empirically-derived regularities in consumer purchasing behavior identified through decades of research at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute (formerly the Marketing Science Centre at the University of South Australia), founded by Andrew Ehrenberg and substantially developed by Byron Sharp. The framework is grounded in unusually rigorous empirical analysis of consumer-panel data across hundreds of categories, brands, and countries. Key empirical regularities include: (1) Double Jeopardy — small brands have fewer customers AND those customers buy slightly less often (challenging segmentation-and-positioning thinking that small brands can compete through loyalty); (2) Duplication of Purchase Law — brands share customers in proportion to brand size, not in proportion to similarity (challenging segmentation thinking); (3) Negative Binomial Distribution (NBD) of purchases — purchase patterns follow predictable mathematical distributions; (4) Light buyers dominate sales — the bulk of any brand's sales come from many occasional buyers, not from few heavy loyal buyers (challenging loyalty-program economics); (5) Penetration drives growth, not loyalty — brands grow primarily by acquiring more customers, not by getting existing customers to buy more. Byron Sharp's How Brands Grow (2010, with Volume 2 in 2016 with Jenni Romaniuk) substantially popularized the framework. Ehrenberg-Bass research challenges substantial parts of the dominant marketing tradition — STP positioning, loyalty programs, segmentation strategies, brand-purpose marketing, and customer-relationship marketing all face empirical pushback from this work. The framework is unusually well-supported empirically by marketing-research standards but has been controversial precisely because its findings challenge what most marketers do.
originators: Andrew S. C. Ehrenberg (foundational, mid-20th century onward); Byron Sharp (substantial contemporary development and popularization); Jenni Romaniuk (subsequent development); broader Ehrenberg-Bass Institute research community
year_or_decade: Ehrenberg's work mid-20th century onward; 2010 (Sharp's How Brands Grow); 2016 (How Brands Grow Volume 2); ongoing institutional research
core_components: Double Jeopardy (small brands have fewer customers who buy slightly less often); Duplication of Purchase Law (brands share customers proportional to size, not similarity); Negative Binomial Distribution of purchases; Light buyers dominate sales; Penetration drives growth more than loyalty; Mental and Physical Availability as key brand-growth drivers; Distinctive Assets (rather than positioning differentiation); Empirically-derived rather than theoretically-deduced; Challenges to STP, loyalty programs, segmentation, brand-purpose marketing; Substantial cross-category and cross-country empirical support
primary_use_case: Brand-growth strategy; foundation for empirically-grounded marketing strategy alternative to STP-based approaches; reference framework in advertising effectiveness research (substantial influence in agencies including BBDO, Anomaly, others); basis for substantial marketing-science research; integration with marketing-mix modeling and econometrics; growing influence in CMO communities seeking empirical foundations; pedagogical framework in marketing-science education programs.
common_criticisms: Specific findings are robust empirically but the strategic prescriptions Sharp draws from them are more contested — critics including Mark Ritson, Peter Field, and Les Binet (the latter two from a different empirical tradition with the IPA databank) argue Ehrenberg-Bass underweights long-term brand-building effects of differentiation and emotional positioning; the framework's pushback against STP and segmentation has been argued to be overstated — some segmentation works even if the bulk of sales comes from broad-market light buyers; works better for low-involvement frequent-purchase categories (FMCG, beverages) than for high-involvement infrequent-purchase categories (cars, financial services); B2B applications are limited by data availability; substantial intra-marketing-science debate continues about the relationship between Ehrenberg-Bass findings and earlier marketing traditions; commercial application sometimes oversimplifies the empirical claims into 'just maximize reach and availability'; the framework's empirical rigor has produced confidence that occasionally outpaces specific findings' generalizability.
primary_sources: Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know; Sharp, B. & Romaniuk, J. (2016). How Brands Grow: Part 2; Ehrenberg, A.S.C. (1959, 1988). Repeat-Buying: Theory and Applications; Ehrenberg-Bass Institute publications (ongoing)

name: Customer Journey Mapping
one_line_summary: Visualizes a customer's stages, touchpoints, emotions, and pain points across an experience.
extended_summary: Customer Journey Mapping is the design-research practice of visually documenting a customer's end-to-end experience with a product, service, or organization across multiple touchpoints, channels, and time periods, surfacing pain points, emotional states, and improvement opportunities. The practice has multiple origins — service-design tradition (Lynn Shostack's service blueprint, 1984; subsequent IDEO and Stanford d.school developments); customer-experience consulting (Forrester, McKinsey, Bain); and the broader design-thinking movement. Modern customer journey maps typically include: stages (awareness, consideration, purchase, onboarding, use, advocacy or similar); touchpoints (website, store, customer service, app, etc.); customer actions, thoughts, and emotions at each stage; pain points and opportunities; metrics and measurement; back-stage processes that support the experience. The mapping process — typically conducted with customer-research input, cross-functional team participation, and visualization workshops — is often as valuable as the artifact for surfacing organizational misalignment about how customers actually experience the company. Customer journey mapping is now standard practice in customer-experience management, service design, and product strategy. The practice integrates closely with personas (separately enriched), empathy mapping (separately enriched), service blueprinting, and design-thinking workflows. Common pitfalls include creating idealized 'happy path' maps that don't reflect actual customer experiences, generating maps without sufficient customer research, and producing artifacts that aren't acted on.
originators: Service-design tradition (Lynn Shostack 1984 service blueprint); design-thinking movement (IDEO, Stanford d.school); customer-experience consulting (Forrester, McKinsey, Bain); subsequent practitioner development through 2000s-2010s
year_or_decade: 1984 (Shostack service blueprint); 2000s-2010s (modern customer journey mapping development); ongoing standardization
core_components: Customer stages (awareness through advocacy or similar); Touchpoints across channels; Customer actions, thoughts, emotions at each stage; Pain points and opportunities; Metrics; Back-stage processes; Cross-functional mapping process; Connection to personas (mapping for specific persona); Connection to service blueprinting (extends mapping with back-stage processes); Integration with design-thinking workflows; Multiple visualization styles (linear journey, cyclical, scenario-based, multi-channel)
primary_use_case: Customer-experience management programs; service-design projects; product-strategy and roadmap development; cross-functional alignment workshops; foundation for customer-experience improvement initiatives; integration with design-thinking and lean-startup workflows; basis for many customer-research projects; growing application in B2B contexts where complex multi-stakeholder journeys need mapping.
common_criticisms: Quality varies enormously — many customer journey maps are aspirational 'happy path' visualizations that don't reflect actual customer experiences; generating maps without sufficient customer research produces decorative artifacts that don't drive insight; maps are often produced and then not acted on, becoming wall-decoration rather than strategy input; the linear-journey-stage framing can underweight the actual non-linear, looping, multi-channel reality of contemporary customer behavior; commercial customer-experience consulting has produced compliance-style customer journey mapping with varying analytical fidelity; tendency to create persona-specific maps that don't aggregate to actual customer-base behavior; integration with quantitative customer behavior data is often weak; B2B journey mapping faces additional complexity (multi-stakeholder buying centers) that single-customer-perspective frameworks don't fully address; emotional-state representations are often based on assumption rather than research; tendency to focus on pre-purchase journey at expense of post-purchase experience.
primary_sources: Shostack, G.L. (1984). 'Designing Services That Deliver', HBR; Stickdorn, M. & Schneider, J. (2010). This Is Service Design Thinking; Kalbach, J. (2016). Mapping Experiences: A Complete Guide to Creating Value through Journeys, Blueprints, and Diagrams

name: Empathy Map
one_line_summary: Visual organizing what a user says, thinks, does, and feels.
extended_summary: The Empathy Map is the design-research visualization tool that captures a customer's experience across multiple dimensions in a structured canvas, used in design-thinking and user-research contexts to develop customer empathy and align team understanding. The tool was articulated by Dave Gray of XPLANE in collaboration with the broader design-thinking community, with the original four-quadrant version (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) emerging in mid-2000s practice and the more elaborate six-section version (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels, plus Pain and Gain) appearing in subsequent iterations. The empathy map is typically arranged around a central representation of a specific customer or persona, with sections capturing: what the customer SAYS (direct quotes, expressed words); THINKS (internal thoughts and beliefs not always expressed); DOES (observable behaviors and actions); FEELS (emotions and emotional states); along with PAINS (frustrations, obstacles, fears) and GAINS (desires, success measures, hopes). The tool is principally used in early-stage design-research synthesis after customer interviews or observation, in cross-functional alignment workshops where teams need to share customer understanding, and as an artifact for ongoing reference during design and development. Empathy maps integrate closely with personas (which provide the 'who') and with customer journey mapping (which provides the 'when and where'). The framework's commercial popularity through Strategyzer (Alexander Osterwalder's company, which produces canvases including the Business Model Canvas, Value Proposition Canvas, and Empathy Map Canvas) has substantially shaped contemporary practice.
originators: Dave Gray (XPLANE, foundational articulation); broader design-thinking community; subsequent commercial development through Strategyzer (Alexander Osterwalder)
core_components: Four original quadrants: Says, Thinks, Does, Feels; Six-section variant adds Pains and Gains; Central customer or persona representation; Application after customer interviews or observation; Cross-functional alignment use; Connection to personas and customer journey mapping; Strategyzer Empathy Map Canvas commercial version; Integration with design-thinking workflows; Distinction between the customer's expressed and internal experience
primary_use_case: Design-research synthesis after customer interviews; cross-functional team alignment workshops; product-strategy and feature-prioritization input; foundation for many design-thinking workshops; integration with personas and customer journey maps; basis for some user-experience design briefs; growing application in B2B and enterprise contexts.
common_criticisms: Distinction between Says-Thinks (internal vs expressed) and Does-Feels (observable vs internal) requires substantial inferential work that researchers often do without sufficient evidence; risk of projecting researcher assumptions about what customers think and feel rather than grounding in actual research; tendency to populate the canvas with general claims rather than specific customer evidence; commercial design-thinking industry has produced compliance-style empathy mapping with varying analytical fidelity; works best when grounded in substantial customer research, with limited value as standalone team brainstorm without research input; the 'empathy' framing can mask the genuine challenge of understanding customers different from oneself; integration with quantitative customer-behavior data is typically weak; multiple competing canvas formats create which-version-when ambiguity; cultural variation in how customers express themselves (high-context vs low-context cultures) affects what 'says' captures; can become decorative artifact rather than strategic input.
primary_sources: Gray, D., Brown, S. & Macanufo, J. (2010). Gamestorming (early empathy-map publication); Osterwalder, A., Pigneur, Y., Bernarda, G. & Smith, A. (2014). Value Proposition Design (Strategyzer Empathy Map Canvas)

name: Personas
one_line_summary: Composite fictional representatives of target user segments used to ground design and marketing.
extended_summary: Personas are fictional representative customers, grounded in research, used to focus product, design, and marketing decisions on specific user types rather than abstract average customers. The practice was substantially developed and popularized by Alan Cooper in his 1999 The Inmates Are Running the Asylum, where he articulated the persona method as a tool for human-computer interaction design — a way to escape 'designing for the elastic user' (everyone, no one). Cooper's foundational personas were detailed fictional characters with names, photos, demographics, goals, behaviors, frustrations, and contexts, developed from user research and used as design targets throughout product development. Subsequent development has produced multiple persona variants: marketing personas (focus on demographics, psychographics, buying behavior); product personas / Cooper-style personas (focus on goals and behavioral patterns); proto-personas (preliminary personas based on team assumptions, to be validated by research); jobs-to-be-done personas (focus on the 'job' the customer hires the product to do, drawing on Christensen's JTBD theory); and many commercial variants. The technique is now standard practice in user-experience design, product management, and marketing strategy, with substantial industry support through tools and templates. Common pitfalls include creating personas based on team assumptions rather than research, generating too many personas (Cooper's recommendation was 1-3 primary personas, not many), focusing on demographics at the expense of behavioral and motivational dimensions, and creating personas that aren't actually used to drive design and marketing decisions.
originators: Alan Cooper (foundational articulation, 1999); subsequent development by Kim Goodwin, Steve Mulder, and broader UX and product-management communities
year_or_decade: 1999 (Cooper's The Inmates Are Running the Asylum); ongoing development through 2000s-2010s
core_components: Fictional representative customers grounded in research; Detailed character description (name, photo, demographics, goals, behaviors, frustrations, context); Use as design and marketing-decision targets; Cooper-style 'goal-directed' personas vs marketing personas vs JTBD personas; Proto-personas for early-stage validation; Recommended 1-3 primary personas (Cooper); Connection to empathy maps and customer journey mapping; Integration with design-thinking and product-management workflows; Distinction from market segmentation (personas are fictional representatives, segments are statistical groupings)
primary_use_case: User-experience design and product management; marketing strategy and content development; cross-functional alignment about target customers; foundation for many product-strategy and design-research processes; integration with customer journey mapping and empathy mapping; basis for many B2B account-based marketing strategies; pedagogical reference in UX and product-management education.
common_criticisms: Personas are often created based on team assumptions rather than substantive research, producing fictional characters that reflect team biases rather than actual customers; tendency to create too many personas (some companies have dozens) reduces focus and decision-making clarity; demographic-heavy personas can underweight behavioral and motivational dimensions that actually drive customer behavior; commercial persona templates and tools have produced compliance-style adoption with varying analytical fidelity; personas that aren't used to drive specific design and marketing decisions become decorative; substantial published critique by Jared Spool and others questioning whether personas drive better decisions than direct user research access; risk of stereotyping when personas embed cultural or demographic assumptions; competing persona methodologies (Cooper, Goodwin, JTBD-based, marketing) create which-version-when ambiguity; integration with quantitative segmentation data is often weak; B2B contexts with multi-stakeholder buying centers complicate single-persona frameworks.
primary_sources: Cooper, A. (1999). The Inmates Are Running the Asylum; Goodwin, K. (2009). Designing for the Digital Age; Mulder, S. & Yaar, Z. (2006). The User Is Always Right

name: Hooked Model
one_line_summary: Eyal's trigger-action-reward-investment loop for habit-forming products.
extended_summary: The Hooked Model was articulated by Nir Eyal in his 2014 book Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products, presenting a four-phase cycle for designing products that create user habits. The phases: (1) Trigger — the prompt that initiates use, either external (notification, email, advertisement) or internal (emotional state, time of day, situation); (2) Action — the simplest behavior in anticipation of reward (scroll feed, tap icon, type message), with the BJ Fogg Behavior Model — B = MAT (Behavior = Motivation, Ability, Trigger) — operationalizing what enables action; (3) Variable Reward — the satisfying outcome of the action, with variability (unpredictability of timing or magnitude) being key to habit formation, drawing on Skinner's variable-reward research; types include rewards of the tribe (social validation), of the hunt (information, resources), of the self (mastery, completion); (4) Investment — the user puts something into the product (data, content, social connections, time, money) that increases the value of subsequent use and primes future triggers. The cycle repeats, building habits as the product becomes increasingly integrated into the user's life. The framework substantially shaped product design at consumer-internet companies in the 2010s, with explicit application to social media, mobile games, and consumer apps. Eyal himself has substantially engaged with subsequent ethical critique — his 2019 Indistractable addressed how users can resist hook-style design, and Eyal has distinguished 'manipulation' (causing actions users would later regret) from 'persuasion' (helping users do what they already want). The framework is craft-substantive but ethically contested, and post-2018 'Time Well Spent' / humane-tech movements have substantially critiqued the design philosophy it embodies.
originators: Nir Eyal; intellectual antecedents in BJ Fogg's behavior model and broader habit-formation research
year_or_decade: 2014 (Hooked); 2019 (Eyal's Indistractable as response to ethical critique); ongoing development
core_components: Four-phase cycle: Trigger, Action, Variable Reward, Investment; External and internal triggers; Connection to BJ Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAT); Variable reward drawing on Skinner research; Three reward types: tribe (social), hunt (resources), self (mastery); Investment increases subsequent value and primes future triggers; Application particularly to social media, mobile games, consumer apps; Subsequent ethical critique and Eyal's response (Indistractable, manipulation vs persuasion distinction); Connection to humane-tech and Time Well Spent movements as critique
primary_use_case: Consumer-product design particularly social media, mobile gaming, consumer apps; foundation for habit-design practices in product management; reference framework in growth-marketing and product-led-growth communities; integration with behavioral-design and persuasive-technology practice; pedagogical reference in product-management and behavioral-economics education; basis for substantial commercial consulting and training business.
common_criticisms: Substantial ethical critique post-2018 about products designed to be habit-forming and the public-health and societal consequences of widespread habit-design (compulsive social media use, attention fragmentation, mental-health concerns particularly among adolescents); Tristan Harris and the Center for Humane Technology have specifically critiqued Hooked-style design philosophy; concerns about manipulation vs persuasion are real — Eyal's distinction between users doing what they already want vs being manipulated into actions they would regret is contested in specific cases; the framework's application to addictive products (social media in particular, where mental-health harms are documented) has prompted Eyal's own subsequent work on resistance (Indistractable); commercial application has produced many products that meet the criteria for harm Eyal himself articulates; concerns about cumulative attentional and societal effects beyond individual product-level analysis; tension between the framework's craft sophistication and its ethical implications; works principally for digital products with frequent-engagement potential; difficulty distinguishing 'hooks' on legitimately useful products from 'hooks' on harmful products; the framework continues to be taught and applied despite substantial public critique.
primary_sources: Eyal, N. (2014). Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products; Eyal, N. (2019). Indistractable (subsequent ethical engagement); Fogg, B.J. (2009). 'A Behavior Model for Persuasive Design' (intellectual antecedent); Center for Humane Technology publications (ongoing critique)
